stem: Match List I (GATT/WTO negotiation round) with List II (distinguishing feature):
listII: Launched in 2001 with development concerns at the centre
Led to the creation of the WTO and brought in services and TRIPS
Produced plurilateral codes on non-tariff barriers such as subsidies and standards
Introduced across-the-board (linear) tariff cuts
explanation: The Kennedy Round moved from item-by-item bargaining to linear tariff cuts, the Tokyo Round negotiated non-tariff codes, the Uruguay Round created the WTO and extended coverage to services and TRIPS, and Doha was launched in 2001 as a development-oriented agenda.

stem: Match List I (IMF term) with List II (description):
listII: Annual review of a member's economic and exchange rate policies
Supplementary international reserve asset allocated to members
Subscription determining voting power and access to financing
Conditional short-term financing for a member facing balance of payments difficulty
explanation: Quota is the subscription that fixes voting power and borrowing access; the SDR is a supplementary reserve asset; Article IV consultation is surveillance; a stand-by arrangement is conditional short-term financing.

stem: Match List I (WTO principle) with List II (meaning):
listII: Publication and notification of trade regulations
Equal treatment of all trading partners
Imported goods treated no less favourably than local goods once inside the market
Commitment not to exceed an agreed ceiling on tariff rates
explanation: MFN means non-discrimination among trading partners, national treatment means non-discrimination between imports and local goods, binding fixes a tariff ceiling, and transparency requires publishing and notifying trade measures.

stem: Arrange the following negotiating rounds and agendas in chronological order:
items: Tokyo Round
Uruguay Round
Kennedy Round
Doha Development Agenda
explanation: The Kennedy Round ran in the mid-1960s, the Tokyo Round in the 1970s, the Uruguay Round from 1986 to 1994, and the Doha Agenda was launched in 2001.

stem: Arrange the following World Bank Group institutions in the order in which they were established:
items: MIGA
IFC
ICSID
IDA
explanation: IFC was set up in 1956, IDA in 1960, ICSID in 1966 and MIGA in 1988.

stem: Arrange the following stages of the WTO dispute settlement process in the correct order:
items: Establishment of a panel
Request for consultations
Circulation of the panel report to members
Adoption of the report by the Dispute Settlement Body
explanation: A dispute starts with consultations; if they fail, a panel is established, its report is circulated to members, and the DSB then adopts it.

stem: Arrange the following developments in the international monetary system in chronological order:
items: Jamaica Agreement legalising floating rates
Creation of the SDR facility
Suspension of the dollar's convertibility into gold
Establishment of the par value system at Bretton Woods
explanation: The par value system dates from 1944, the SDR from 1969, the suspension of dollar-gold convertibility from 1971 and the Jamaica Agreement from 1976.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) of India?
options: It is a criminal statute under which every contravention attracts imprisonment
It requires prior approval for every current account transaction
It replaced FERA, 1973 and seeks to facilitate external trade and the orderly development of the foreign exchange market
It deals only with foreign investment and not with foreign exchange dealings
explanation: FEMA replaced the more restrictive FERA, 1973, with a facilitative objective and a civil, penalty-based approach to contraventions. Current account transactions are generally free, and the Act covers foreign exchange dealings as well as investment.

stem: Which of the following is an accommodating (compensatory) item in a country's balance of payments?
options: Import of machinery by a manufacturer
Remittances sent home by migrant workers
Foreign direct investment attracted by profit opportunities
Drawing down official foreign exchange reserves to cover a deficit
explanation: Accommodating items are undertaken to finance a deficit or surplus arising from other transactions, for example a fall in reserves. Imports, remittances and profit-driven FDI are autonomous transactions.

stem: A country records the following (₹ crore): merchandise exports 400, merchandise imports 520, service receipts 180, service payments 110, net private transfer receipts 60 and net investment income payments 30 (an outflow). Its current account balance is:
explanation: Trade balance = 400 - 520 = -120; net services = 180 - 110 = +70; net transfers = +60; net income = -30. Total = -120 + 70 + 60 - 30 = -20, a deficit of 20.

stem: The spot rate is ₹51 per unit of a foreign currency. One-year interest rates are 4 per cent in India and 2 per cent in the foreign country. According to covered interest rate parity, the one-year forward rate should be:
explanation: Forward = Spot × (1 + i domestic) / (1 + i foreign) = 51 × 1.04 / 1.02 = 53.04 / 1.02 = ₹52.00. The foreign currency trades at a forward premium because the domestic interest rate is higher.

stem: A bank quotes ₹82.00–₹82.40 per US dollar (bid–ask). An exporter sells US$10,000 to the bank. The rupees received by the exporter are:
explanation: The bank buys dollars at its bid rate of ₹82.00, so the exporter receives 10,000 × 82.00 = ₹8,20,000. The ask rate of ₹82.40 applies when the bank sells dollars.

stem: The spot rate is ₹80 per US dollar and the dollar is at an annualised forward premium of 6 per cent for three months. The three-month forward rate is:
explanation: Premium for three months = 6% × 3/12 = 1.5%. Forward rate = 80 × 1.015 = ₹81.20. Using the full 6% gives 84.80, and a discount would give 78.80.

stem: The rupee moves from ₹80 to ₹100 per US dollar. Measured by the change in the dollar value of one rupee, the rupee has depreciated by:
explanation: One rupee was worth $1/80 = 0.0125 and is now worth $1/100 = 0.0100. The fall is 0.0025/0.0125 = 20%. The dollar's appreciation of 25% is a different measure.

stem: For a country, the price elasticity of demand for its exports is 0.6 and for its imports is 0.3 (trade initially balanced). According to the Marshall–Lerner condition, a depreciation of its currency will:
options: Worsen the trade balance, because the sum of the elasticities is less than one
Improve the trade balance, because both elasticities are positive
Leave the trade balance unchanged, because the elasticities are unequal
Improve the trade balance, because the export elasticity exceeds the import elasticity
explanation: Depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of the elasticities exceeds one. Here 0.6 + 0.3 = 0.9 < 1, so the volume gain is too small to offset the higher rupee cost of imports.

stem: In a country's Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index, where a rise denotes real appreciation, an increase in the index indicates:
options: Improved price competitiveness of the country's exports
A loss of price competitiveness against its trading partners
A fall in the country's foreign exchange reserves
A fall in the country's nominal exchange rate against the dollar
explanation: REER is a trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted index. A rise means the currency has appreciated in real terms, making home goods relatively dearer and reducing competitiveness.

stem: Assertion (A): A country's balance of payments always balances in the accounting sense.
reason: Reason (R): Every international transaction is recorded on the double-entry principle, with an equal credit and debit.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Each transaction has a matching credit and debit entry, so total credits equal total debits. Imbalances appear only within sub-accounts, not in the total.

stem: Assertion (A): Covered interest arbitrage tends to keep the forward premium or discount close to the interest rate differential between two currencies.
reason: Reason (R): Both hedgers and speculators participate in the forward exchange market.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true, but the link between forward rates and interest differentials comes from riskless arbitrage, not from the mere presence of hedgers and speculators.

stem: Assertion (A): An Indian importer with a dollar payable can protect itself against rupee depreciation by buying dollars forward.
reason: Reason (R): A forward contract gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy the currency at the agreed rate.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Buying forward fixes the rupee cost of the payable, so A is true. A forward contract is a binding obligation on both parties; the right without obligation describes an option, so R is false.

stem: Assertion (A): A depreciation of a country's currency always improves its trade balance immediately.
reason: Reason (R): Because of the J-curve effect, the trade balance may worsen in the short run after a depreciation before it improves.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Trade volumes adjust slowly, while the import bill rises at once, so the balance can deteriorate first. A is therefore false and R is true.

stem: Assertion (A): A country can have a current account deficit and still record an overall balance of payments surplus.
reason: Reason (R): Net capital and financial account inflows can exceed the current account deficit, adding to foreign exchange reserves.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The overall balance depends on the current account plus net capital and financial flows. When inflows exceed the deficit, reserves rise, which is exactly how an overall surplus arises.

stem: Assertion (A): Under a clean (pure) floating exchange rate system, the central bank continuously intervenes to hold the rate at a target level.
reason: Reason (R): Under a clean float, the exchange rate is determined by the demand for and supply of currencies in the market.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A clean float involves no central bank intervention, so A is false. R correctly states that market demand and supply set the rate.

stem: Consider the following statements about the balance of payments:
items: The balance of trade records only merchandise (visible) exports and imports.
The current account balance equals the balance of trade plus net services, income and transfers.
A deficit in the balance of trade necessarily means an overall balance of payments deficit.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A trade deficit can be offset by surpluses in services or transfers or by capital inflows, so it does not necessarily imply an overall deficit.

stem: Consider the following statements about the foreign exchange market:
items: In a spot transaction, delivery of the currencies normally takes place within two working days.
A forward rate is agreed today for delivery of currency on a specified future date.
Under a direct quote, a forward premium on the foreign currency means the forward rate is higher than the spot rate.
A forward contract can be cancelled at will without any cost to the customer.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. A forward contract is binding, and early cancellation involves charges or settlement of any difference at market rates.

stem: Consider the following statements about the effect of exchange rate changes on the trade balance:
items: The Marshall–Lerner condition says depreciation improves the trade balance if the sum of the demand elasticities for exports and imports exceeds one.
The J-curve describes a trade balance that worsens immediately after depreciation before improving.
If both export and import demand are perfectly inelastic, depreciation will improve the trade balance.
The elasticity approach stresses the effect of relative price changes on trade flows.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. With perfectly inelastic demand, volumes do not respond, so depreciation only raises the domestic cost of imports and worsens the balance.

stem: Consider the following statements about foreign exchange regulation in India:
items: FEMA, 1999 replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973.
Contraventions under FEMA are treated as civil in nature rather than as criminal offences.
Under FEMA, current account transactions are generally permitted unless specifically restricted, while capital account transactions are regulated.
FEMA makes it an offence to deal in foreign exchange through anyone other than the RBI itself.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. FEMA permits dealing through authorised persons such as authorised dealer banks, so statement 4 is false.

stem: Consider the following statements about changes in the value of a currency:
items: Devaluation is an official reduction in the par value of a currency under a fixed exchange rate system.
Depreciation under a floating exchange rate system is announced by the government through an official order.
Revaluation is an official increase in the par value of a currency.
Devaluation makes imports cheaper in terms of the domestic currency.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Depreciation under a float results from market forces rather than an official order, and devaluation makes imports dearer in domestic currency.

stem: Consider the following statements about balance of payments disequilibrium and its correction:
items: Cyclical disequilibrium arises mainly from permanent changes in the structure of an economy's production.
Structural disequilibrium arises from changes in demand or supply conditions, such as a shift in the pattern of production or tastes.
Under the gold standard, the price-specie flow mechanism was the automatic route to balance of payments adjustment.
Expenditure-reducing and expenditure-switching policies are both used to correct a deficit.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct. Cyclical disequilibrium comes from differences in the phase of business cycles between countries, not from permanent structural change.

stem: Match List I (international transaction) with List II (balance of payments category):
listI: Receipts from exports of IT services
Inflow of foreign direct investment into an Indian company
listII: Current transfers
Merchandise trade
Capital or financial account
Services
explanation: Textile exports are merchandise trade, IT exports are services, gift remittances are current transfers, and FDI inflow is a capital or financial account item.

stem: Match List I (exchange rate regime) with List II (feature):
listII: Parity adjusted periodically in small, pre-announced steps
Rate set by market forces with occasional central bank intervention
Rate held at a declared parity by the central bank
Rate determined purely by demand and supply without intervention
explanation: A peg holds a declared parity; a clean float involves no intervention; a managed float allows occasional intervention; a crawling peg changes the parity in small, announced steps.

stem: Match List I (theory or condition) with List II (core idea):
listI: Monetary approach to the balance of payments
listII: Forward premium or discount reflects the interest rate differential
Exchange rate adjusts to the relative price levels of two countries
Depreciation improves the trade balance only if the sum of demand elasticities exceeds one
A payments deficit arises when domestic money supply exceeds money demand
explanation: PPP links exchange rates to relative price levels, interest rate parity links forward margins to interest differentials, Marshall–Lerner is an elasticity condition, and the monetary approach treats a deficit as excess money supply.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (description):
listII: Bank permitted to deal in foreign exchange with customers
Law governing foreign exchange transactions in India, replacing FERA
Apex regulator that issues rules and manages the foreign exchange market under FEMA
Association of banks dealing in foreign exchange, framing rules on rates and practices
explanation: FEDAI is the association of authorised dealer banks, the RBI is the regulator under FEMA, an authorised dealer is a bank permitted to deal in foreign exchange, and FEMA is the governing statute.

stem: Arrange the following in the order in which they governed the rupee's exchange rate:
items: Unified market-determined exchange rate
Link to a basket of currencies
Dual exchange rate under LERMS
Link to the pound sterling
explanation: The rupee was linked to sterling until 1975, then to a basket of currencies, then moved to the dual rate of LERMS in 1992, and to a unified market-determined rate in 1993.

stem: Arrange the following events in Indian foreign exchange history in chronological order:
items: Enactment of FEMA
Devaluation of the rupee (1966)
Acceptance of IMF Article VIII obligations
Enactment of FERA
explanation: The devaluation came in 1966, FERA was enacted in 1973, India accepted Article VIII obligations (current account convertibility) in 1994, and FEMA followed in 1999.

stem: Under a floating exchange rate system, arrange the steps by which a current account deficit tends to correct itself:
items: Domestic goods become cheaper for foreigners and imports become dearer
A current account deficit creates an excess supply of domestic currency
The domestic currency depreciates
The deficit narrows as exports rise and imports fall
explanation: The deficit creates excess supply of the domestic currency, which depreciates; the price effect on exports and imports then narrows the deficit.

stem: Arrange the steps of the gold-standard price-specie flow mechanism in the correct order:
items: Gold flows out of the deficit country
Domestic prices fall, improving export competitiveness
The country runs a payments deficit
Money supply in the deficit country contracts
explanation: A deficit causes gold outflow, which shrinks the money supply, lowers prices and so restores export competitiveness.
